meta.title: Burmese A1 Beginner
meta.subtitle: 500 words · both directions, as two cards per word
meta.desc: Both study directions in one deck: Burmese → English (see the Burmese, recall the meaning) and English → Burmese (see an English meaning, recall the Burmese). Each direction is a card of its own with its own schedule, so recognising a word and producing it are learnt separately. 500 words for a beginner, aligned to A1 of the Common European Framework of Reference, whose global descriptor begins 'Can understand and use familiar everyday expressions and very basic phrases aimed at the satisfaction of needs of a concrete type' — a learner here is able to introduce themselves and others, to ask and answer questions about personal details such as where they live, people they know and things they have, and to interact in a simple way provided the other person talks slowly and clearly and is prepared to help. WHERE THESE WORDS COME FROM, since it matters: no exam board publishes a graded word list for Burmese, so this deck is not any examination's vocabulary and does not claim to be. It is assembled from two things that can be stated. 416 of the 500 come from a vocabulary written for the level's scope — greetings and politeness, the pronouns (a man's and a woman's), the question words and the particles of the spoken language every sentence is built out of, people and the family, numbers and the commonest counting words, time and the days of the week, food and drink, money and shopping, clothes, the home, the town and getting about, the body and feeling ill, the weather and nature, colours, animals, school and work, the everyday verbs and the describing verbs — and the other 84 are the commonest remaining words of the Burmese Wikipedia. Burmese writes no spaces between words, so that text was cut into words against the dictionary, and only words of two syllables or more are taken from the count (a one-syllable count also holds every piece the cut could not place). Burmese has two registers, the written and the spoken; this deck teaches the SPOKEN one (တယ်, ရဲ့, နဲ့, ဒီ), while Wikipedia is written in the literary one (သည်, ၏, နှင့်, ဤ), whose particles are left for a later level — and its fill is encyclopaedic in places (government, history, religion). The cards are dealt by that frequency, so the words met most often come first. Only words English Wiktionary has an entry for can be taught here. Every word is in the Myanmar script, as Burmese is written; the Alphabet deck, first in this collection, teaches the letters and the tone marks. Beneath each word is its pronunciation in the International Phonetic Alphabet, as Wiktionary gives it, with the four tones marked: à low, á high, a̰ creaky, aʔ checked (short, with a catch). Many short Burmese words are several words in one spelling, so a card shows the meanings of the part of speech it teaches (ကို, the object particle; ငါး, five and fish). A noun shows the classifier it is counted with where Wiktionary names one. Example sentences are few: 236 of the 500 words have one, from Wiktionary's usage examples and from Tatoeba, which holds about 590 Burmese sentences; none is invented. There is no speaker button: few devices have a Burmese voice. Sources. Level: the Common European Framework of Reference (Council of Europe), global scale. Meanings, pronunciation and classifiers: English Wiktionary, via the kaikki.org extraction (CC BY-SA 4.0). Frequency: the Burmese Wikipedia, articles of the 2026-11-01 dump (CC BY-SA 4.0). Example sentences: English Wiktionary (CC BY-SA 4.0) and Tatoeba (tatoeba.org), CC BY 2.0 FR.
